results.title: Kids Calling Girls 'Foids' At School? You Need To Pull Them Up On It
results.description: A derogatory slur aimed at women has made its way into the vocabulary of teens. The term ‘foid’, made popular among online misogynistic communities, has entered the mainstream with parents and researchers noting some kids are now saying it. Girls have shared stories of teen brothers saying it. One parent shared on Reddit that their 16-year-old son “used to talk about girls like a normal teenager but now he says things like ‘foids only respect you if you jestermaxx correctly’ which I had to search and it made me feel sick”. Another Redditor revealed they’d stopped playing games online and planned to delete their social media accounts because of it. “How in the world do kids know this term? What happened for it to become so popular all of a sudden?” they asked. Unfortunately, ‘foid’ is just another harmful word being used to degrade girls and women. A 15-year-old student wrote for The Guardian earlier this year how boys were using the term “female” to “degrade us and equate us to animals”. “We’re also ‘thots’ (whores), ‘community pussy’ and ‘bops’,” she added. (The latter is an offensive term used to call girls or women promiscuous.) What is a ‘foid’? Speaking to Joeli Brearley and Elliott Rae on their To Be A Boy podcast this week, Meadhbh Park, the author of Blackpilled, said: “I have come across cases where a young person was outwardly saying how women have too much power, and women are stupid, and calling them ‘foid’ ...” She described ‘foid’ as being like “female robot” or “android”, adding: “So basically, women have no humanity, they’re actually just stupid robots who go along with what they’re told by the media.” This tracks with what Wired noted in an article: “Women were disparaged as ‘female humanoids,’ then ‘femoids,’ and finally just ‘foids’.” If boys are using this language, calling girls ‘females’ or ‘bops’, or being outwardly mean towards girls in their class, experts say it’s definitely worth exploring with them. How to talk to kids about it “As parents, we cannot let conversations about misogyny slide, particularly given how it’s rapidly changing the landscape for children, teens and young people,” family therapist Fiona Yassin told HuffPost UK. “The severity of misogyny is great and we cannot ignore it.” Instead of responding instinctively with “don’t say that!” or “do you know what you just said?” (which can shut down the conversation rather than open it up), the founder and clinical director of The Wave Clinic suggested saying something like: “Hey, I just heard you use this word. I’d like to understand what you think it means when you’re using it.” You can then sit down with them and, using short simple sentences, explain what it means. “This gentle approach works across age groups and invites dialogue. For younger boys, we can explain that it’s an unkind word that doesn’t belong in kind interactions: ‘Foids’ isn’t a fun or silly word – it’s mean, offensive and harmful,” she explained. “With older children, we can begin to introduce the concept of misogyny and explain how this word diminishes respect for a group of people. Its cultural implications are significant, and it’s important that children understand that. Again, explanations should always be age-appropriate.” It’s important to bear in mind that because the word’s becoming normalised online, some children – especially younger ones – might be repeating it innocently, without an understanding of what it actually means. “But others will know exactly what it means, and for them, it may carry intent,” added the therapist. “That intent could be disrespectful, bullying, belittling, or shaming. It could even be part of a broader campaign of unkindness targeting certain groups of children and young people. This makes it all the more important for adults to intervene.” Offering support if your child was called a ‘foid’ If your child was called a foid by someone else – whether online or at school – parents must intervene here, too. Especially if they feel targeted or attacked. “Support your child by helping them find firm, respectful responses – something like, ‘I’m not available for that kind of language,’” said Yassin. “Also, acknowledge how hurtful this can be. Parents need to be aware of the emotional impact this word can have, and ensure their children feel safe and supported.” Keep an eye out for behaviour changes For kids who show consistent behaviour based on resentment, jealousy and a feeling of inadequacy, Park urged parents to intervene. Sometimes kids might become quiet and spend a lot more time online – this can be a red flag. In this case, Park advised checking their computers or phones, regardless of the discomfort that might initially bring. She spoke of how there are new groups popping up called nihilistic violent extremists, which she described as “like incels on steroids”. “These groups are also teaching kids how to use VPNs, how to go on torrents, how to scrape other people’s details and hack them and dox them ... their ability, unfortunately, to conceal their own stuff from their parents is getting better,” she explained. “So it’s really difficult and complicated but you do have to, as much as you can, lay down the law if you are concerned about your boy who has suddenly become very quiet online ... “Best situation is he’s having fun on a game, worst situation is he’s in these very popular spaces online.” If you’re concerned that your child is being radicalised online, speak to their school who can make a referral to Prevent, which works to protect vulnerable people from being exploited by extremists. results.title: Beyond Prayer: Making Room for Mental Health Conversations
results.description: Why psychological wellbeing deserves a place in our everyday church conversationsMughalu T KinimiWe often encourage people to pray when they are struggling. We remind them to trust God when life becomes difficult, seek spiritual strength when they feel weak, and turn to the church when they encounter personal crises. These are meaningful aspects of Christian life. Yet, an important question deserves greater attention: How often do our churches openly discuss mental health? How well are we equipped to recognise psychological distress, and do we know when someone needs professional help? Mental health remains an uncomfortable subject in many communities. Although awareness is gradually increasing, conversations about depression, anxiety, trauma and other psychological difficulties are still not sufficiently integrated into everyday religious and community life. In some situations, unusual behaviour, emotional disturbances or psychological struggles are interpreted primarily through the language of spiritual oppression or demonic influence. While spiritual beliefs are important to many Christians, the tendency to rely exclusively on such explanations can sometimes prevent people from considering other dimensions of human suffering. This is not an argument against prayer, spiritual healing or the church's ministry. Rather, it is an invitation to consider whether our understanding of human suffering has become too narrow. The language we use shapes how we understand sufferingCommunication plays an important role in shaping how individuals and communities interpret their experiences. The words we use to describe a person's condition can influence how families respond, where they seek assistance and how the wider community treats that individual. For instance, when someone experiences prolonged sleeplessness, unusual behaviour, emotional instability or disorientation, the immediate interpretation may sometimes be spiritual. The family might seek prayer and deliverance, believing that the person is experiencing spiritual oppression. Such responses may come from genuine concern and sincere faith. However, these symptoms can also be associated with psychological conditions, neurological complications, physical illnesses or a combination of factors. Consider someone who begins displaying unusual behaviour following a serious accident. A change in behaviour, disturbed sleep, memory difficulties or repetitive speech could warrant neurological and psychological assessment. Interpreting these symptoms exclusively as spiritual disturbance risks overlooking conditions that require medical attention. The difficulty is not that people pray. The difficulty arises when prayer becomes the only response considered. Our explanations matter because they shape our actions. When a particular explanation dominates public conversation, other possibilities can become invisible. Consequently, the individual may receive spiritual attention but remain without the medical or psychological support necessary for recovery. The church as a communication environmentThe church is more than a religious institution. It is also a significant communication environment where people learn how to understand themselves, their relationships and the challenges they encounter in life. Through sermons, prayer meetings, pastoral counselling, fellowship groups and other forms of communication, churches influence the language communities use to interpret human experiences. There are encouraging developments. In a telephonic enquiry with a counsellor at Lapiye Mental Well-being (5th Mile Junction, Dimapur, adjacent to Green Park), I was informed that churches are gradually beginning to talk about mental health. This is a welcome development and deserves recognition. However, the conversation needs to move beyond occasional awareness programmes and become part of regular church teaching and pastoral practice. Church leaders, in particular, have an important responsibility. Their influence extends beyond theological instruction. They help shape attitudes towards suffering, illness, relationships and personal struggles. When mental health is rarely discussed from the pulpit, congregations may continue to perceive it as an unfamiliar or uncomfortable subject. Imagine if churches regularly addressed depression, anxiety, trauma, emotional exhaustion and psychological wellbeing alongside other aspects of Christian living. Such conversations could help people recognise signs of distress, reduce stigma and understand that seeking professional assistance is not a failure of faith. Pastors do not need to become psychiatrists or psychologists. However, they should be equipped to recognise warning signs, respond compassionately and refer individuals to appropriate professionals when necessary. Beyond the separation of faith and medical careOne of the challenges in discussing mental health within Christian communities is the tendency to perceive spiritual care and professional treatment as competing approaches. This creates an unnecessary divide. Prayer can provide comfort, hope and a sense of belonging. Pastoral counselling can offer spiritual guidance and emotional support. At the same time, psychological counselling, psychiatric treatment and medical intervention can address conditions that require professional care. These approaches need not be mutually exclusive. A more holistic understanding of human wellbeing requires us to recognise that human beings are embodied persons. Our spiritual experiences are lived through our bodies, brains, emotions, memories and relationships. Psychological distress cannot always be separated from physical conditions, just as spiritual wellbeing cannot be understood independently of our social and relational lives. This calls for what may be described as Embodied Christian Discernment: an approach to understanding human suffering without reducing it to a single explanatory category. Such discernment recognises four interconnected dimensions:• Psychological: Mental health, cognition, trauma and emotional wellbeing.• Biological: The brain, body, neurological conditions and physical health.• Spiritual: Faith, prayer, pastoral care and religious meaning.• Communal: Family, belonging, social support and collective responsibility. These dimensions are not isolated compartments. They interact in shaping human experiences. A person experiencing psychological distress may also have an underlying physical condition, require spiritual support and depend on the care of family and community. Embodied Christian discernment does not dismiss spiritual realities, nor does it attempt to explain every human experience through medical categories. Rather, it encourages careful listening, responsible interpretation and appropriate responses. It reminds us that recognising a medical or psychological condition does not diminish a person's faith. Towards a more informed and compassionate churchIf churches are to become meaningful spaces of care, mental health education must become part of their regular ministry. Pastors and church leaders can organise awareness programmes, invite mental health professionals to speak, provide safe spaces for confidential conversations and establish referral networks with qualified practitioners. Families and congregations must also learn to respond without immediately labelling individuals or treating their conditions as a source of shame. People experiencing psychological difficulties need understanding and appropriate care, not public speculation or premature judgement. Ultimately, this responsibility extends beyond the church. Families, educational institutions, healthcare providers and the wider community must work together to create an environment where mental health can be discussed openly. The Christian commitment to caring for others should include the whole person. If we believe that human life has dignity and value, then the psychological and emotional dimensions of that life deserve our attention alongside its physical and spiritual dimensions. Perhaps the question we need to ask is not whether we have enough faith to pray for those who suffer, but whether we have enough understanding to recognise the different forms their suffering may take. The church must not become a place where every unexplained human struggle receives only a spiritual explanation. It should become a community where every suffering person encounters understanding, compassion, responsible discernment and appropriate care. Faith should never be a barrier to seeking help. Rather, it should inspire us to care more deeply for the whole person.

results.title: A call from the bank, a letter from the SNB—this is how scammers try to get your money
results.description: Criminals are using a new scam to try to swindle bank customers in Switzerland out of their money. They warn of allegedly unauthorized transfers and send out fake letters purporting to be from the Swiss National Bank. Ultimately, the victims are supposed to withdraw cash and hand it over.
